newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippine economy growth hopes look out of reach.
newsitem.headline: Philippine economy growth hopes look out of reach.

text.p: Asia's latest would-be Tiger economy, the Philippines, looks unlikely to meet optimistic growth targets this year after first quarter figures released on Thursday failed to hit the mark, economists said.

"It seems to me that the government will have a hard time catching up (with its target for the year). We will be lucky to hit six percent for the whole year," Raul Ruiz, research head of Sun Hung Kai Securities, said.

The government says it is on track for seven to eight percent gross national product growth this year, despite announcing a slightly disappointing 6.1 percent rise in the first three months of the year, down from 6.9 percent in the same period last year.
The level is also lower than the government's own projection of a 6.4 percent growth for the period.
However, Planning Secretary Cielito Habito remained bullish that the whole year target would be attainable.
A booming service and a growing agriculture sector would more than compensate for a slackening manufacturing sector which account for a quarter of total domestic output.
But it only grew 2.3 percent in the first quarter, less than half the rate last year, as many firms revamped their operations to cope with steep competition from abroad.
They were forced to shift to high value products, Habito said, but added the transition would eventually bring better income to these companies.
However, Noel Reyes, research head of Anscor Hagedorn Securities, said the slowdown had already started last year and a recovery should be in the offing by now.
"We were counting on the recovery in the manufacturing this year. It's getting worse. We are disappointed by the slowdown," he said.
The economy will have to perform exceptionally well in the next few months to hit the government target, he said.
Growth of a little less than 7.0 percent was more likely, which means flat growth from last year's 6.94 percent growth.
"Personally, I think the targets are on the high side. But then again, this is their (the government's) targets. This is not a projection," Dennis Lapid, economist of Vickers Ballas Securities, said.
Another concern was the marked slowdown in the income sent home by the 6.5 million or so Filipinos working abroad, which grew only 32.5 percent against 75.5 percent last year.
Manuel Goseco, economist of Dharmala Securities, said at least the first quarter figures erased any fears that the country would go the way of Thailand.
Philippine financial markets have been hammered over the past two months by investor concerns that its economy was about to emulate some of Thailand's recent economic troubles.
Relatively robust growth figures for the first three months should dispel speculations about the health of the economy, he said.
